difficultyReason: Medical argument with a hidden reference-class shift: the trial measured a surrogate biomarker in one population, but the conclusion generalizes to a clinical outcome in a broader, older population. Tempting distractors include a too-strong universal, a shift-in-subject about alternative mechanisms, and a reversed-direction trap. Negation test requires re-identifying what the researchers actually measured.
stimulus: Cardiologist: In our six-week trial, adults aged 40 to 55 who took the drug Noviran had, on average, measurably lower resting blood pressure than those who took a placebo. Since sustained high blood pressure is a leading cause of stroke in older adults, physicians should prescribe Noviran to their patients over 70 to reduce those patients' risk of stroke.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the cardiologist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any intervention that lowers blood pressure in middle-aged adults will lower blood pressure by a comparable margin in adults over 70.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Noviran has no side effects in older adults that outweigh its benefits for stroke prevention.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Noviran's effect on blood pressure in middle-aged adults is not attributable solely to mechanisms that cease to operate in adults over 70.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most adults over 70 who suffer strokes have had elevated blood pressure for an extended period before the stroke.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No drug currently prescribed to adults over 70 lowers blood pressure more effectively than Noviran.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from 'Noviran lowered blood pressure in 40-to-55-year-olds' to 'Noviran will reduce stroke risk in people over 70.' That requires the drug still to lower blood pressure in the older group. Negate C: the mechanism by which Noviran lowers blood pressure in middle-aged adults ceases to operate in people over 70. Then the trial data no longer supports any stroke-risk claim about over-70s, and the conclusion collapses. C is therefore necessary — stated defensively, ruling out the specific alternative that the drug simply doesn't work in the target population.
explanations.A: Too strong and shifted. The argument doesn't need 'any intervention' to work comparably — only Noviran. A universal claim about all blood-pressure-lowering interventions is not required.
explanations.B: Out of scope. Side-effect balance is a separate prudential question, not a link in the inflammation-to-stroke inference. Negating B (there are worse side effects) would make prescribing imprudent but would not undermine the reasoning from trial data to stroke-risk reduction.
explanations.D: Reversed direction. The argument needs lowering blood pressure to reduce stroke risk, not that stroke patients previously had high blood pressure. Negating D leaves the argument intact.
explanations.E: Out of scope and too strong. Relative efficacy against other drugs is not what the conclusion depends on; Noviran could be second-best and the stroke-reduction claim could still hold.

difficultyReason: Environmental science stimulus with a counterfactual trap. The recovery of the fish population after the pollution-control policy is being credited to the policy itself; the necessary assumption rules out a non-policy explanation (prior natural rebound already underway). Close-cousin distractors include a too-strong comparison claim and an out-of-scope observation about other species.
stimulus: Environmental scientist: Five years after Lake Halberg's watershed council imposed strict limits on agricultural runoff, the lake's yellow perch population, which had declined for decades, had rebounded to near its historical average. The council's chair credits the limits with the recovery. Since nothing else changed about the lake's management in that period, the chair's explanation is almost certainly correct.
questionStem: The scientist's argument depends on the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: runoff limits of comparable strictness have produced measurable fish recoveries in other lakes with similar pollution profiles

choices.label: B
choices.text: the yellow perch population would not have rebounded to near its historical average during those five years had the runoff limits not been imposed

choices.label: C
choices.text: agricultural runoff was the single largest source of pollution in Lake Halberg prior to the limits

choices.label: D
choices.text: no other species in Lake Halberg declined during the five years following the imposition of the limits

choices.label: E
choices.text: the watershed council enforced the runoff limits consistently throughout the entire five-year period

explanations.correct: To credit the limits with the recovery, the scientist must assume the recovery would not have happened without them. Negate B: the perch would have rebounded to near the historical average over those five years even without the limits (for example, a long-delayed natural cycle). Then the post-policy recovery is not evidence that the policy caused it, and the chair's explanation is undercut. B is thus the indispensable counterfactual bridge.
explanations.A: Shift in subject and too strong. Other lakes' responses are not a premise of the argument; the conclusion is about Lake Halberg specifically. Negating A leaves this lake's situation unchanged.
explanations.C: Too strong. The limits could have caused the recovery even if runoff was not the single largest pollution source — only that limiting it made the difference. Negating C does not destroy the argument.
explanations.D: Out of scope. Other species' trajectories are not a link in the reasoning about perch recovery.
explanations.E: Tempting but not strictly necessary. Even inconsistent enforcement could have produced the rebound if sufficient overall; the argument needs only that the limits (however enforced) made the difference, not that enforcement was consistent throughout.

difficultyReason: Economic argument with a comparative-claim subtlety. The conclusion says Brindale has a lower cost of living than Coverdale, but the evidence is that Brindale residents spend less on housing and groceries. The necessary assumption is that the non-measured categories do not make up the difference — a defensive assumption easily overlooked in favor of more aggressive-sounding distractors.
stimulus: Economist: Residents of Brindale spend, on average, a smaller share of their income on housing and groceries than residents of Coverdale do. Since housing and groceries are among the largest household expenses in both cities, the overall cost of living in Brindale must be lower than that in Coverdale.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the economist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Residents of Brindale do not spend a sufficiently larger share of their income on expenses other than housing and groceries to offset the difference in housing and grocery spending.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Housing and groceries together account for more than half of an average household's spending in both Brindale and Coverdale.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Residents of Brindale earn, on average, the same income as residents of Coverdale.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any city in which housing and groceries consume a smaller share of income than in Coverdale has a lower overall cost of living than Coverdale.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Brindale's housing and grocery prices are lower in absolute terms than those in Coverdale.

explanations.correct: The conclusion compares overall cost of living. The premises compare only housing and groceries. Negate A: Brindale residents spend enough more on other categories to offset the housing-and-grocery savings. Then overall cost of living in Brindale is not lower, and the conclusion fails. A is necessary — a classic defensive, gap-closing assumption.
explanations.B: Close cousin but not required. The argument needs only that the offset not erase the difference, not any specific threshold share. The argument could hold even if housing plus groceries were less than half of total spending.
explanations.C: Shift in subject. The comparison is of shares of income, not absolute income. Equal income is not needed for the share-based inference to yield a cost-of-living conclusion.
explanations.D: Too strong. This is a general principle that would prove the conclusion rather than merely enabling it; necessary assumptions are narrower. It is a sufficient-assumption, not necessary-assumption, answer.
explanations.E: Shift in subject. The premises are about share of income, not absolute prices. Negating E (absolute prices are equal or higher in Brindale) does not block the argument, which works off share-of-income data.

difficultyReason: Legal argument with a statistical-inference gap. The prosecutor infers from a matching DNA profile that the defendant was present; the necessary assumption constrains the reference class — specifically, that the profile is not shared by a substantial number of other people who could plausibly have been at the scene. Distractors include a reversed-direction assumption and a too-strong uniqueness claim.
stimulus: Prosecutor: DNA extracted from a hair found at the crime scene matches the defendant's genetic profile on all thirteen markers tested. Profiles matching on all thirteen markers are extremely rare in the general population. We should therefore conclude that the hair came from the defendant, placing him at the scene.
questionStem: The prosecutor's argument requires the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: the hair could not have been transferred to the scene by someone other than the person it came from

choices.label: B
choices.text: the thirteen markers tested are the markers least likely to coincide by chance in unrelated individuals

choices.label: C
choices.text: the population from which potential contributors to the hair would plausibly be drawn is not substantially enriched in people sharing the defendant's thirteen-marker profile

choices.label: D
choices.text: the defendant has no identical twin living within the city where the crime occurred

choices.label: E
choices.text: the matching profile alone constitutes sufficient evidence to convict the defendant of the crime

explanations.correct: The argument hinges on the rarity of a thirteen-marker match in the general population. But what matters is rarity in the reference class of people who could plausibly have contributed the hair. Negate C: that reference class is substantially enriched in matching profiles (for example, because the defendant's close relatives live nearby and were frequent visitors). Then the match is no longer strong evidence that the hair is the defendant's, and the conclusion collapses. C fills the reference-class gap.
explanations.A: Out of scope for this conclusion. The conclusion is that the hair came from the defendant, placing him at the scene; secondary transfer is a separate issue from source identification.
explanations.B: Too strong. The argument doesn't need the thirteen markers to be the best possible choice, only that a match on them be rare enough in the relevant population.
explanations.D: Close cousin, but narrower than necessary. The problem of enriched reference-class matches is broader than identical twins; ruling out only twins leaves other enrichment sources (close relatives, an isolated subpopulation) unaddressed.
explanations.E: Shift in subject. Whether the match suffices for conviction is a legal-standard question, not a premise of the source-identification inference.

difficultyReason: History stimulus with a chronology-dependent gap. The historian dates a trade network from merchandise found in a shipwreck, but the conclusion requires that the ship sank while the merchandise was in active trade, not long after. Distractors include a too-strong claim about trade routes and a reversed-direction temporal claim.
stimulus: Historian: Amphorae bearing stamps that were used only by vintners in the port city of Rhodion between 140 and 110 B.C.E. have been recovered from a shipwreck off the coast of Sicily. The amphorae still contained residues of Rhodian wine when found. We conclude that a commercial wine trade connecting Rhodion to western Mediterranean markets was active during the second half of the second century B.C.E.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rhodian vintners did not export wine to western Mediterranean markets at any time before 140 B.C.E.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The ship carrying the amphorae sank no more than a few decades after the amphorae were filled.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The stamps used by Rhodian vintners after 110 B.C.E. differed from those used during 140 to 110 B.C.E.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No stamped Rhodian amphorae from the period in question have been recovered from sites outside the western Mediterranean.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rhodian wine was the most valuable cargo commonly shipped to western Mediterranean ports during the period in question.

explanations.correct: The dating premise is the stamps' production window, 140 to 110 B.C.E. To conclude that the wine trade was active in that window, the historian must assume the shipwreck occurred close to that window rather than long afterward. Negate B: the ship sank two centuries later, perhaps while transporting antique-filled amphorae for some unrelated purpose. Then the wreck's existence does not establish an active second-century trade, and the conclusion falls apart. B is the necessary chronological bridge — parallel to the lake-sediment bones case.
explanations.A: Shift in subject. The conclusion concerns whether the trade was active in 140 to 110 B.C.E., not whether it was uniquely active then. Earlier trade is compatible with the conclusion.
explanations.C: Close cousin, but not required. Even if later stamps were identical, the stamps recovered could still plausibly be from the 140 to 110 B.C.E. window. The argument can work without ruling out later identical stamps, provided B holds.
explanations.D: Too strong and out of scope. Whether other amphorae surface elsewhere is independent of whether this wreck establishes the trade.
explanations.E: Out of scope. Relative cargo value is not a premise of the argument.

difficultyReason: Technology stimulus with a hidden reference-class issue: benchmark tests on a processor were run under controlled lab conditions, but the conclusion generalizes to everyday performance. The necessary assumption rules out the alternative that the lab conditions favored the tested chip in ways not replicated in typical use. Distractors include a shift-in-subject comparison and a too-strong universal.
stimulus: Technology reviewer: In our laboratory benchmarks, the Aster X7 processor completed standard computational tasks, on average, 18 percent faster than the leading competitor's chip. Because these benchmarks are the accepted industry standard for gauging processor speed, consumers should expect the Aster X7 to handle their everyday computing needs noticeably more quickly than the competitor's chip handles them.
questionStem: The reviewer's argument depends on the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: the Aster X7 is priced competitively with the leading competitor's chip

choices.label: B
choices.text: the conditions under which the laboratory benchmarks were run did not give the Aster X7 an advantage that is absent in typical everyday computing use

choices.label: C
choices.text: no other processor currently sold to consumers performs better on the industry-standard benchmarks than the Aster X7

choices.label: D
choices.text: every task that consumers commonly perform on a personal computer is included in the industry-standard benchmark suite

choices.label: E
choices.text: consumers typically choose processors on the basis of laboratory benchmark performance rather than on the basis of other considerations

explanations.correct: The argument extrapolates from controlled benchmarks to everyday performance. That extrapolation requires that the benchmark setup not have favored the Aster X7 in ways absent from normal use (for example, thermal management tuned to the benchmarks, or minimal background processes). Negate B: the lab conditions did favor the Aster X7 in ways absent from everyday use. Then the 18-percent advantage would not transfer to consumer settings, and the conclusion falls apart.
explanations.A: Out of scope. Pricing is irrelevant to whether the processor handles tasks more quickly; the conclusion is about speed, not value.
explanations.C: Too strong and shifted. The conclusion compares the Aster X7 to 'the leading competitor's chip,' not to all other processors. Negating C does not block the argument.
explanations.D: Too strong. The argument needs only that benchmark performance reasonably predict everyday performance, not that every common task appear in the suite. Negating D (some tasks are missing) does not destroy the argument provided the suite is reasonably representative.
explanations.E: Shift in subject. The conclusion is a prediction about what consumers should expect, not about how consumers in fact choose. Consumer purchasing criteria are orthogonal to the speed claim.

difficultyReason: Linguistics stimulus with a scope-narrowing gap. The corpus shows a vocabulary contraction, but the conclusion generalizes to speakers' actual vocabulary knowledge. The necessary assumption rules out the possibility that the corpus is unrepresentative of general usage. Trap answers include a too-strong universal and a reversed-direction claim about written versus spoken language.
stimulus: Linguist: A study of text messages sent by teenagers over the past twenty years finds that the average number of distinct English words appearing in a year's worth of messages has declined by roughly 15 percent. We conclude that the working vocabulary of the average English-speaking teenager has contracted correspondingly over the same period.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the linguist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The contraction in the number of distinct words appearing in teenagers' text messages does not primarily reflect shifts in what teenagers choose to write about in messages rather than in what words they know.

choices.label: B
choices.text: English-speaking teenagers today send, on average, approximately the same number of text messages per year as teenagers did twenty years ago.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every word known by a teenager has some probability of appearing in a year's worth of that teenager's text messages.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Teenagers whose working vocabularies contract are also the teenagers whose text messages contain the fewest distinct words.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The vocabularies used by teenagers in text messages are a larger subset of their overall vocabularies than are the vocabularies they use in spoken conversation.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from corpus evidence (distinct words in messages) to a claim about working vocabulary. If the contraction reflects a narrowing of message topics rather than a narrowing of known words, then the corpus is not a valid proxy for working vocabulary. Negate A — the contraction does primarily reflect topic shift — and the conclusion collapses. A is the narrow, defensively phrased bridge required.
explanations.B: Close cousin, but not strictly necessary. Even if teenagers send fewer or more messages today, the distinct-word count per year could still track vocabulary. The argument can survive a moderate change in message volume.
explanations.C: Too strong. The argument doesn't need every word to have some chance of appearing — only that the sample be representative enough for the comparison.
explanations.D: Reversed direction. This states how vocabulary contraction correlates with corpus data, not what the argument requires to move from corpus data to vocabulary.
explanations.E: Out of scope. The argument is about text-message corpora, not a comparison between written and spoken vocabularies. Negating E does not break the inference.

difficultyReason: Ethics stimulus with a counterfactual gap. The ethicist concludes the sanctions policy was morally justified on the grounds that it achieved its stated aim. The necessary assumption is that the aim could not have been achieved by an alternative with less serious harm. Tempting wrong answers include a too-strong impossibility claim and a shift-in-subject about general sanctions theory.
stimulus: Ethicist: The economic sanctions imposed by nation A on nation B succeeded in compelling nation B's government to abandon its program of forced labor. The sanctions also caused meaningful hardship for many civilians in nation B who had no role in the program. Nevertheless, because the sanctions accomplished their stated aim, imposing them was morally justified.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the ethicist's argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No alternative measure available to nation A would have compelled nation B's government to abandon the forced-labor program while causing less hardship to uninvolved civilians.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Economic sanctions are, in general, morally justified whenever they succeed in achieving their stated aim.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The hardship caused to uninvolved civilians in nation B was not foreseeable by nation A at the time the sanctions were imposed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nation B's government would not have abandoned the forced-labor program in the absence of the sanctions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The forced-labor program caused harm to nation B's civilians at least as severe as the hardship imposed by the sanctions.

explanations.correct: The ethicist must bridge 'sanctions achieved the aim' to 'sanctions were justified' given that they harmed civilians. A policy with avoidable collateral harm is hard to call justified if a less harmful alternative would have worked. Negate A: an alternative was available that would have succeeded with less civilian hardship. Then the sanctions' collateral harm was avoidable, and their justification evaporates. A is the necessary assumption.
explanations.B: Too strong — a universal principle about sanctions. Necessary assumptions are narrow; the argument needs only this case, not a general rule. This is a sufficient-assumption trap.
explanations.C: Close cousin, but not required. Foreseeability affects blame but not whether these sanctions were justified given the alternatives available. The argument can be defended even if the hardship was foreseeable, so long as A holds.
explanations.D: Tempting as a counterfactual but concerns effectiveness, which is already granted. The sanctions are stipulated to have succeeded; the argument does not additionally need that the program would have continued otherwise.
explanations.E: Shift in subject. A comparison of severity between forced labor and sanctions hardship is not a link in the argument as stated; the argument rests on the achievement of the aim plus justification. Negating E does not block A's reasoning.

difficultyReason: Policy argument with a statistical-inference subtlety. The analyst infers that the tutoring program raised test scores from a year-over-year jump at participating schools; the necessary assumption rules out a confounding change that coincided with the program. Distractors include a too-strong claim about causation in general and a shift-in-subject about non-participating schools.
stimulus: Policy analyst: After the state launched its after-school tutoring initiative, participating schools saw standardized math scores rise by an average of 9 percent in a single year — a jump far larger than any observed in the preceding decade. Since the initiative is the most salient change at these schools over that time, the initiative must be responsible for the jump.
questionStem: The analyst's argument requires the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: no factor other than the tutoring initiative that could plausibly have produced the jump in math scores changed at the participating schools during that year

choices.label: B
choices.text: the tutoring initiative increased math scores at every individual school that participated in it

choices.label: C
choices.text: schools that did not participate in the tutoring initiative did not see any comparable jump in math scores during the same year

choices.label: D
choices.text: standardized math scores are a reliable indicator of students' overall academic achievement

choices.label: E
choices.text: the tutoring initiative will continue to raise math scores in subsequent years if funding is maintained

explanations.correct: The argument infers causation from a coincident change, reasoning that the initiative is 'the most salient change.' That inference holds only if no other plausible cause changed too. Negate A: another plausible cause (for example, a simultaneous curriculum overhaul) did change at those schools. Then the initiative is not uniquely positioned to explain the jump, and the conclusion fails. A is the necessary alternative-cause-ruled-out assumption.
explanations.B: Too strong. The conclusion concerns average improvement, not school-by-school uniformity. Some participating schools could have seen no gain while the average still rose.
explanations.C: Close cousin. It would strengthen the argument, but it is not required: the initiative could still be responsible for the participating-school jump even if other forces independently produced a comparable jump elsewhere. Necessary-assumption answers do not usually require this kind of comparison across populations.
explanations.D: Shift in subject. The conclusion is about the score jump, not about overall academic achievement. Score reliability for broader claims is not a premise here.
explanations.E: Out of scope. The conclusion is about what happened, not about what will happen in later years.

difficultyReason: Arts argument with a comparative-claim gap. The critic concludes a novelist is the greatest of her generation based on literary-prize tallies over a period, but the conclusion requires that the prizes track greatness and that the comparison population is her generation. Tempting wrong answers include a reversed-direction claim and a too-strong universal about prize-giving.
stimulus: Literary critic: Over the past two decades, Mira Adelaide has received more major international literary prizes than any other novelist writing in English during that period. These prizes are awarded by expert panels specifically to recognize the highest literary achievement. We can therefore conclude that Adelaide is the greatest English-language novelist of her generation.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the critic's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A novelist who writes in a language other than English cannot belong to Adelaide's generation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The major international literary prizes awarded over the past two decades tracked literary achievement at least as reliably among English-language novelists of Adelaide's generation as among those of other generations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Adelaide's generation of English-language novelists is represented among the novelists who received major international literary prizes over the past two decades.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No novelist writing in English over the past two decades who did not receive as many major international prizes as Adelaide achieved as much as she did in literary terms.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The expert panels awarding the major international literary prizes over the past two decades consisted of members drawn from diverse national and cultural backgrounds.

explanations.correct: The argument needs the prize-tally lead to translate into a greatness lead over Adelaide's generation. Negate D: some other English-language novelist of the past two decades, with fewer prizes, in fact achieved more in literary terms than Adelaide. Then Adelaide is not the greatest of her generation, and the conclusion fails. D is the necessary defensive bridge — phrased as 'no one uncredited surpassed her.'
explanations.A: Shift in subject and too strong. The conclusion concerns English-language novelists, but restricting Adelaide's generation to English speakers is not required by the argument; it would alter the conclusion's scope rather than support it.
explanations.B: Close cousin but inverted. The argument does not need a cross-generational reliability comparison; it needs only that within Adelaide's generation, the prizes track greatness well enough for her tally lead to correspond to a greatness lead — which is what D establishes.
explanations.C: Necessary-sounding but vacuous: Adelaide herself is an English-language novelist of her generation who received prizes, so representation is guaranteed by the stimulus. C adds nothing the argument needs.
explanations.E: Out of scope. Panel diversity is not a link in the argument; the stimulus already asserts that the panels are expert and award for literary achievement.
